Chevron's FY2025 10-K says extended periods of low prices can have a material adverse impact on its results, financial condition and liquidity. It says upstream earnings, cash flows, capital spending, production and proved reserves could suffer, and upstream assets could be impaired. Downstream earnings could also be hurt. It also says liquidity pressure could affect credit ratings and financing costs, and that downturns could slow investment, including in New Energies. Management says sustained lower prices could lead to impairments, operating expense cuts (including employee reductions) and capital expenditure changes. For context, FY2025 net income was about $12.3 billion, down 30.4% from FY2024, and operating cash flow rose 7.8% to about $33.9 billion. In the 10-K risk-factor and MD&A text retrieved, Chevron did not quantify the effect of a prolonged low-price scenario.
Chevron's FY2025 10-K says extended periods of low prices or demand for crude oil, natural gas and NGLs have had, and can in future have, a material adverse impact on its results of operations, financial condition and liquidity. It names crude oil, natural gas and NGL prices as the most significant factor affecting its results.
Chevron says low prices could negatively affect its upstream earnings, cash flows and capital expenditure programs, as well as its production and proved reserves, and that upstream assets may become impaired. Downstream earnings could also be hurt because they depend on refined product supply, demand and margins.
Chevron warns that a significant or sustained decline in liquidity could adversely affect its credit ratings, potentially increase financing costs and reduce access to capital markets. It also says downturns may slow the pace and scale at which it can invest in its business, including New Energies.
In MD&A, Chevron states that periods of sustained lower commodity prices could result in the impairment or write-off of specific assets. It could also lead the company to adjust operating expenses, including employee reductions, and capital expenditures, along with other measures to improve financial performance. The Q2 2026 10-Q repeats this language.
Chevron says impairment determinations rest on highly uncertain estimates, such as future commodity prices and the supply-and-demand outlook. It also says a sensitivity analysis of earnings under other impairment assumptions is not practicable. The retrieved 10-K text therefore gives no quantified impairment impact for a prolonged low-price scenario.
Chevron's FY2025 net income was about $12.3 billion.
Net income fell about 30.4% in FY2025 from FY2024. This is historical context, not proof that prices caused the change.
Operating cash flow rose about 7.8% in FY2025 from FY2024, to about $33.9 billion.
Chevron attributed the 2025 increase in operating cash flow to higher cash distributions from TCO and contributions from legacy Hess assets, which more than offset the impact of lower commodity prices.
Chevron's shareholder distributions in 2025 were an annual dividend of $6.84 per share (the 38th consecutive annual increase) and $12.1 billion of share repurchases. The retrieved passages do not say how these would change under prolonged low prices.
